issues.description: The manuscript claims to use a 'national probability sample' and a 'nationally representative sample' throughout the abstract, introduction, and discussion, but the Methods section reveals participants were recruited through 'the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.' A university psychology participant pool is neither nationally representative nor a probability sample. This is a fundamental and pervasive misrepresentation of the sample that undermines the generalizability claims made throughout the paper.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The sample has a mean age of 19 years at Time 1 and is drawn from an introductory psychology pool, making it effectively a student sample. Yet the paper repeatedly contrasts its findings with Stanley et al.'s [14] student sample, claiming the current study's general population sample explains different results. The current sample is functionally identical to the student sample it is being contrasted with, invalidating this key interpretive argument.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female... It is likely that the difference in sample type therefore accounts for the differences in our results, as we used a general population sample.

issues.description: The paper references the NZAVS (New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study) website for full sample details and syntax, and acknowledges the NZAVS team in the acknowledgments, yet the Methods section describes recruitment through a university psychology participant pool. The NZAVS is a genuine national probability sample of adults, while a psychology pool is not. It is unclear which dataset is actually being used, creating serious confusion about the sample's nature and origin.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website... We express our gratitude to the New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS) team for their work collecting and maintaining the NZAVS.

issues.subcategory: Construct label mismatch between abstract/introduction and results
issues.description: The abstract and introduction describe the outcome variable as 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' and 'willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment,' while the measures section describes 'concern about environmental problems' with items about concern and perceived exaggeration. The results and figures then label this variable as 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment' (WILL). These are distinct constructs (behavioral intention vs. environmental concern vs. sacrifice willingness) and the operationalization does not clearly match any of the labels used.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people's willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment... Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems... SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001)

issues.description: The environmentalism measure is described as consisting of only two items modelled from Liu and Sibley's scale, one measuring concern and one measuring perceived exaggeration (reverse-scored presumably). Two items are insufficient for reliable latent variable measurement, and the paper does not explain how these two conceptually distinct items (concern vs. denial of exaggeration) are combined into a single composite. No factor structure, inter-item correlation, or justification for treating them as a unidimensional scale is provided.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: Only six items from the SDO scale are used, and the paper does not specify which six items were selected from the full SDO6 scale, nor whether they represent both the dominance and anti-egalitarianism subscales. The selection procedure and psychometric justification for this abbreviated measure are not reported. Given that Stanley et al. [24] (cited in the paper) found that the two dimensions of SDO differentially predict environmentalism, collapsing them without justification is a validity concern.
issues.quote: Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto's [1] SDO6 scale. Three items favoured dominance, such as 'To get ahead in life, it is sometimes okay to step on other groups', and three favoured equality, such as 'We should have increased social equality'.

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but included at all other time points. This creates measurement non-equivalence across waves, which is particularly problematic in a cross-lagged model that assumes stationarity and constrains parameters to equality across time. The authors do not address how this missing item affects the reliability or validity of the RWA composite at Time 2, nor whether measurement invariance was tested.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The reported RMSEA 90% confidence interval [.025, .026] is implausibly narrow (a range of only .001) for a model of this complexity and cannot be correct. A confidence interval this narrow would be essentially impossible in practice and suggests a reporting error. The point estimate of .03 falls outside this reported interval, which is internally inconsistent.

In reporting path coefficients, the authors use 'SD' to denote what are clearly standard errors of the regression coefficients (e.g., SD = .01 for a path coefficient of B = -.11). Standard deviations of regression coefficients are not a standard reporting metric; these values are standard errors. This is a systematic mislabeling throughout the results section that could confuse readers and misrepresents the precision of the estimates.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])

issues.subcategory: RWA confidence interval inconsistent with significance claim
issues.description: The RWA cross-lagged path to environmentalism is reported as B = -.02, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]. However, the lower bound of the CI is -.01, which is extremely close to zero, and the upper bound is -.05. This CI appears to be reported in the wrong order (should be [-.05, -.01] with -.05 being more negative). More critically, if the SE is .01 and B = -.02, a 95% CI would be approximately [-.04, .00], which would include zero and contradict the p = .001 claim. The numbers are internally inconsistent.

The chi-square difference test comparing the SDO-to-RWA path versus RWA-to-SDO path is reported as χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. This value is extraordinarily large for a single degree of freedom test in a model with 374 participants and is almost certainly a reporting error. Such a value would indicate a catastrophic model misfit for a single parameter constraint, which is implausible given the other fit statistics reported.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.subcategory: Chi-square test used to compare non-nested models inappropriately
issues.description: The authors use chi-square difference tests to compare the relative strength of cross-lagged paths (e.g., SDO→environmentalism vs. environmentalism→SDO). While constraining paths to equality and comparing model fit is a legitimate approach, the authors simultaneously claim 'the traditional Wald test... is not possible' due to model constraints, yet then proceed to use what is effectively a likelihood ratio test. The rationale for why the Wald test is impossible but the chi-square difference test is valid is not explained.
issues.quote: Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible. Instead, we imposed similar constraints on the model as in the Wald test: we constrained the paths to equality from SDO to environmentalism and from RWA to environmentalism.

issues.subcategory: Contradiction between model comparison result and interpretation
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the model with SDO and RWA paths constrained to equality versus the unconstrained model yields χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126, which is non-significant. The authors acknowledge this but then proceed to interpret SDO as a 'stronger predictor' based on the pattern of coefficients alone. This is inconsistent: the formal test fails to reject the null hypothesis of equal predictive strength, yet the authors draw conclusions about differential prediction.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The authors use listwise deletion to handle missing data in a five-wave longitudinal study. With five time points, listwise deletion is likely to result in substantial data loss and can introduce bias if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR). The authors do not report how many participants were lost due to listwise deletion, do not test the MCAR assumption, and do not justify this approach over full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation, which are standard in longitudinal SEM.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The paper reports 374 participants across five time points but provides no information about the original sample size, attrition rates at each wave, reasons for dropout, or whether those who dropped out differed systematically from those who remained. In a five-year longitudinal study, attrition is a critical threat to validity. The absence of any attrition analysis makes it impossible to evaluate whether the retained sample is representative even of the original (already non-representative) sample.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European). Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The cross-lagged panel model assumes that constructs are measured equivalently across all five time points. The authors constrain autoregressive and cross-lagged paths to equality (stationarity assumption) but do not report testing measurement invariance of the factor loadings and intercepts across waves. Without establishing configural, metric, and scalar invariance, comparisons of latent means and cross-lagged paths across time are not valid.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: Traditional CLPM used without random-intercept consideration
issues.description: The authors use a traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM), which is known to confound within-person and between-person effects, potentially producing spurious cross-lagged paths. The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) is now considered the methodological standard for separating trait-level stability from within-person dynamics. The authors do not acknowledge this limitation or justify their choice of the traditional CLPM.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.subcategory: Causal language from correlational longitudinal data
issues.description: Despite acknowledging in the introduction that cross-sectional data cannot support causal claims, the discussion repeatedly uses causal language based on the cross-lagged panel model results. Cross-lagged panel models do not establish causation; they establish temporal precedence under strong assumptions that are not tested here. The authors' own bidirectionality findings further complicate causal interpretation.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism... With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: The authors briefly mention that a third variable could explain the bidirectional relationships but treat this as a minor alternative explanation rather than a fundamental threat to their causal claims. Key confounders such as political conservatism, religiosity, socioeconomic status, and personality traits (e.g., openness to experience) that predict both ideological attitudes and environmentalism are not measured or controlled for in the model.
issues.quote: Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable... Future research could test these and other alternative explanations by examining whether the ideology-environmentalism link is explained by perceptions of resource scarcity or economic downturn.

issues.subcategory: Missing degrees of freedom for chi-square
issues.description: The chi-square symbol and degrees of freedom are rendered as plain '2(1)' and '2(279)' throughout the results section, suggesting a formatting error where the chi-square symbol (χ²) was lost. More importantly, the degrees of freedom for the overall model chi-square (χ²(2279) = 36511.73) are extremely large, suggesting a very complex model, but the authors do not explain how 2279 degrees of freedom arise from a model with 3 variables across 5 time points, making replication impossible.

The authors state that stability paths are shown in Figure 1 but do not report the actual numerical values of the autoregressive coefficients in the text. Given that stability is a key prediction of the study and the figure is not reproduced in the manuscript text provided, readers cannot evaluate the magnitude of stability effects without access to the figure.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but Figure 1's caption states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are different thresholds, and it is unclear which was actually used. This inconsistency raises concerns about post-hoc threshold adjustment.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.subcategory: Missing inter-wave correlations and descriptive statistics
issues.description: Table 1 presents only Time 1 descriptive statistics and correlations. For a five-wave longitudinal study, means, standard deviations, and reliabilities at each wave are essential for evaluating measurement consistency and potential floor/ceiling effects over time. The cross-wave correlations are also absent, making it impossible to assess the degree of stability empirically from the reported data.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: The study involves multiple analytical decisions (choice of constraints, significance thresholds, model specification, handling of missing items) with no pre-registration reported. The post-hoc nature of some decisions (e.g., the chi-square difference test as a substitute for the Wald test, the interpretation of non-significant model comparison as supporting differential prediction) suggests undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom that could inflate false positive rates.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The authors report constraining cross-lagged paths to equality twice in the same paragraph, suggesting a copy-paste error that may reflect unclear thinking about the model specification. More substantively, the decision to impose stationarity constraints is presented as a preference rather than a tested assumption, and the authors do not report whether a non-stationary model was tested and rejected.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.subcategory: Overclaim of generalizability given sample homogeneity
issues.description: Even setting aside the student pool recruitment issue, the sample is 86% Pākehā (New Zealand European) and 76% New Zealand-born, with a mean age of 19. The authors claim results are 'highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population,' but this homogeneous, young, predominantly European sample cannot be considered representative of New Zealand's diverse population, which includes significant Māori, Pacific, and Asian communities.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: Misapplication of Duckitt's model to explain SDO-RWA asymmetry
issues.description: The authors interpret the finding that RWA predicts SDO but not vice versa as evidence that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' However, Duckitt et al.'s [23] model cited by the authors actually predicts that in authoritarian-conservative societies, RWA should predict SDO more strongly—which is what was found. The authors' interpretation ('socialized into authoritarianism') is a novel claim not directly supported by the cited theory and conflates the direction of cross-lagged effects with socialization processes.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander's are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: In the introduction, the authors predict 'reciprocal cross-time effects' between SDO and RWA based on Duckitt's [3] cognitive consistency argument. However, the results show a unidirectional effect (RWA→SDO only), which the authors then explain using Duckitt et al. [23] as if this was expected. The post-hoc reframing of a disconfirmed prediction as consistent with theory is not acknowledged as such.
issues.quote: Therefore, on the association between SDO and RWA over time, we expect reciprocal cross-time effects... Whilst the lagged effect of RWA on SDO was statistically significant... SDO did not predict change in RWA... This contradicted our initial expectations, however it is consistent with Duckitt et al. [23]

issues.subcategory: Contradictory description of significance threshold rationale
issues.description: The authors justify adopting p < .05 'because of the large sample size of this dataset,' which is the opposite of standard practice. Large samples increase statistical power and make it easier to detect trivially small effects as significant, which typically motivates using a more stringent threshold (e.g., p < .01 or p < .001), not a more lenient one. The stated rationale is logically inverted.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: Willingness to sacrifice vs. environmental concern conflation
issues.description: The paper's stated focus is on 'willingness to change behaviour' and 'willingness to make sacrifices,' but the actual measure items assess concern ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?') and perceived exaggeration ('To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'). Concern and behavioral willingness are empirically and conceptually distinct constructs. This conflation runs throughout the paper and affects the validity of all substantive conclusions.
issues.quote: Our study specifically examines the influence of SDO and RWA on people's willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment... Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems.

issues.description: The authors dismiss the poor CFI (.86, below the conventional .90 threshold) by attributing it to model complexity, while accepting the model based on RMSEA and SRMR. However, they do not report TLI (which also penalizes for complexity), do not discuss what the poor CFI implies for the model's adequacy, and do not compare fit to alternative model specifications. Selectively reporting fit indices that support model acceptance without addressing those that do not is a reporting bias.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.
